note.headline: Apple's Returns on Capital Keep Widening While the Price Runs Ahead of Every Model We Run
why: The June quarter, reported 30 Jul 2026, beat on both lines: earnings per share of US$2.02 against a US$1.89 consensus, a 6.9% surprise, on revenue of US$109.4b that came in 0.3% ahead. That is the thirteenth beat in thirteen scored quarters, a 100% record that says more about how the company guides than about how it trades.

Return on invested capital reached 51.9% against a weighted average cost of capital we put at 8.9% — a spread of 43%, the widest of the ten filed years, and the tenth consecutive year above the hurdle. The average spread across the run is 23.9%. Very few businesses of this size sustain anything close to it.

The shares change hands at US$309.35 against a US$191.80 fair value estimate, a 1.61 price/fair value. Every one of the ten models behind that estimate lands below the current price; the most generous, a price/earnings multiple, stops at US$250.97.

Our quant rating is Hold, grade B, 2.98 of 5 across 75 ranked ratios. Profitability carries it at A- and 3.95 while valuation drags at C- and 1.69, and the arithmetic between those two poles is most of the rating. This is a top-percentile operating business priced above most of its own sector: the trailing P/E of 35.3x sits behind 59% of the Technology sector, EV/EBITDA of 27.2x behind 71%.
note.bottomLine: We rate Apple Hold on the quant scale — grade B, 2.98 of 5 across 75 ranked ratios. A profitability score of 3.95, top-percentile in the Technology sector on every measure of return on capital, is pulled back by a valuation score of 1.69, and the composite lands just above the middle. We read the business as wide-moat, with ten of ten filed years earning more on capital than that capital cost. Separately, the shares screen overvalued at US$309.35, 61.3% above a US$191.80 fair value estimate; on a Low uncertainty band they would read undervalued only below US$153.44. Nothing in the operating record argues against this company. The argument is about what has already been paid for it.

strategy: Apple turned over US$466.8b in the trailing twelve months and converted 27.6% of it into net income, employing 166.0k people to do so. The gross margin stands at 48.7% and the operating margin at 33.2%. Those three figures together describe a business that is unusual less for its size than for the fact that scale has not diluted it: the company is roughly twice as large as it was a decade ago and materially more profitable per unit of revenue than it was then.

The revenue mix is concentrated and the concentration is the central fact about the company. iPhone accounts for 50.4% of revenue at US$209.6b, and Service for 26.2% at US$109.2b. Wearables, Home and Accessories contributes 8.6%, Mac 8.1% and iPad 6.7%. More than half of what the company earns therefore depends on one product line, and any forecast for Apple is in large part a forecast for that line and for the installed base it creates.

The second half of that mix matters more than its share suggests. Services revenue is earned off devices already sold, carries no bill of materials, and is the most plausible explanation for a gross margin that has moved from 39.1% in 2016 to 46.9% in 2025. Hardware sold at a premium does not, on its own, widen a margin by nearly eight points across a decade in which component costs and currencies both moved against the industry.

Geographically the business is less concentrated than the product mix. The Americas segment accounts for 42.9% of revenue, Europe 26.7%, Greater China 15.5%, the rest of Asia Pacific 8.1% and Japan 6.9%. The Greater China share is the line most worth watching: it is large enough to matter to consolidated growth and it is the one region where the company faces both a determined domestic competitor set and a policy environment it does not control.

Across the ten filed years to 2025 revenue compounded from US$215.6b to US$416.2b while the operating margin widened from 27.8% to 32%. Research and development spending rose over the same span from US$10.05b to US$34.55b. That is the shape of a company reinvesting heavily and still expanding its margin, which is the combination operating leverage is supposed to produce and very rarely does at this scale.

Looking forward we take the consensus path as filed rather than substituting a house view. The 30 analysts covering the company expect revenue to compound at 9% a year and earnings per share at 11.5% from fiscal 2026 to 2029, well above the 3% a year revenue compounded between fiscal 2021 and fiscal 2025. Earnings outrunning revenue assumes the margin keeps widening, as it has across the filed run. We note the consensus outer years thin out as coverage does; the tail is used unsmoothed and should be read as an estimate, not a plan.
bulls: Return on invested capital of 51.9% has exceeded our estimate of the cost of that capital in ten of the last ten filed years, by an average of 23.9% and by 43% in the most recent one — a record of value creation that almost nothing of this size matches.

The services line now contributes 26.2% of revenue at US$109.2b, and the shift toward it has lifted the gross margin from 39.1% to 46.9% across the filed run while the operating margin widened from 27.8% to 32%.

The balance sheet carries no strain: net debt is 0.3x EBITDA, the Altman Z-score is 12.49 and the Piotroski score 9 of 9, and the company still returned US$106.1b to shareholders in the latest filed year.
bears: The valuation is the whole of the bear case and it is not marginal: 42.3x book ranks in the bottom 4% of the Technology sector, and against a US$191.80 fair value estimate the shares trade at a 1.61 price/fair value — every one of the ten models kept in the estimate lands below the market price.

Half the business is one product: iPhone is 50.4% of revenue, and a further 15.5% of consolidated revenue is earned in Greater China, so two concentrations that can move together account for a large share of the forecast.

The balance sheet is efficient rather than conservative — a current ratio of 1.00 ranks in the bottom 9% of the sector and equity funds just 28% of assets, in the bottom 14%, both consequences of returning more cash than the business generates.
moat: We assign Apple a wide economic moat rating. Return on invested capital has exceeded our estimate of the company's weighted average cost of capital in ten of the last ten filed years, by an average of 23.9%. In the most recent year the spread was 43% — return on invested capital of 51.9% against a cost of capital of 8.9% — and it is the widest of the run. A record that consistent is not the product of a good decade in an end market. Something is defending it.

What that something is, on the evidence available here, is the combination of a device business that commands a price premium and a services business earned off the devices already in circulation. Services are 26.2% of revenue at US$109.2b and require no unit to be manufactured. That is the mechanism by which the gross margin moved from 39.1% to 46.9% across the filed run, and it is also why the margin is unusually stable: the standard deviation of gross margin across those ten years is 3.5%.

Margin stability of that order through a decade containing a pandemic, a component shortage and a substantial currency cycle is itself the evidence. A price-taker's gross margin moves with its input costs. This one did not, which says the company has not had to buy its volume, and pricing power held through a full cycle is the most durable form of competitive advantage there is.

A word on which return figure to read. Return on equity is 137.2% and return on assets 33.6%, both top-percentile, but the first of those is substantially flattered: a decade of buybacks has left equity funding only 28% of assets, and a thin equity base lifts return on equity without the business improving at all. Return on invested capital, at 51.9%, counts debt and equity alike and is the honest read. It is the one we rate the moat on.

What would erode it is visible in the same numbers. Half of revenue sits in a single product line, and a moat that rests on an ecosystem is only as durable as the reason to stay inside it. Reinvestment has been heavy — research and development rose from US$10.05b to US$34.55b across the run — which is consistent with a company that understands the position has to be defended rather than merely harvested, but heavy spending is a cost of the moat and not proof of it.

The stated limit on this rating matters more than usual here. Morningstar's wide rating is a forecast that excess returns persist for twenty years. This one is a measurement of ten years that have already happened, and no arithmetic over filed accounts can make the forward claim. A company whose advantage is about to be competed away still measures wide on this evidence. Read it as the record a moat rating would be built from, not as the rating itself.
fairValue: Our fair value estimate is US$191.80 a share, the median of ten models. Thirteen were run; three were set aside because they do not describe this company. The price/book multiple returned US$26.93, but a return on equity of 137% means book value is a small part of what the business earns on. The price/sales and EV/revenue multiples, at US$123.44 and US$138.07, assume sector margins, and Apple keeps 28% of sales as profit against a sector median of 9%. The ten that remain span US$140.71 to US$250.97, with the middle half between US$177.49 and US$225.25.

At US$309.35 the shares trade on 35.3x trailing earnings and 35x forward, on an enterprise value of 27.2x EBITDA, for a free cash flow yield of 3%. That is a 1.61 price/fair value, 61.3% above the estimate. Every one of the ten models lands below the traded price, and the most generous of them, a price/earnings multiple at the Technology median of 28.6x, stops at US$250.97. A buyer at today's price is paying for something none of the models sees.

The profit drivers explain what that something would have to be. Between fiscal 2021 and fiscal 2025 operating profit rose from US$108.9b to US$133.1b. Of the US$24.1b added, US$15.0b came from selling more at the old margin of 29.8%, and US$9.1b from the margin widening to 32.0%. Service supplied 81% of the revenue added, growing from US$68.4b to US$109.2b and from 19% of revenue to 26%. Gross margin rose from 41.8% to 46.9% even as research and development rose from 6.0% of revenue to 8.3%: the mix paid for the spending.

Which models deserve weight. The two 10-year discounted cash flows, at US$193.07 on terminal growth and US$185.95 on a revenue exit, are the most informative: they take five analyst years, grow five more from the median forecast step and fade to 2.5%, and 58% and 57% of their value rests on the terminal year. The earnings multiples bracket them, EV/EBITDA at US$190.53 on 16.9x and EV/EBIT at US$225.39 on 21.6x. The consensus they rest on has revenue compounding at 9% a year from fiscal 2026 to 2029 and earnings per share at 11.5%, so it assumes the margin widens a little further still.

The parameter that matters most is the discount rate. Every cash flow model uses 9.0%, built mostly from a cost of equity of 9.1% that reflects a beta of 1.09, and on the median model 70% of the value rests on the years after the forecast. The bull case, which reruns the cash flows on the highest revenue any analyst publishes, reaches US$205.37, still 33.6% below the price. The price therefore implies growth beyond the consensus horizon, margins wider than the consensus, or a lower cost of capital than the market charges for a share this stable. The analyst price target, at US$340.72, answers a different question: where the stock will trade.

None of this feeds the quant rating, which grades Apple against its sector and is Hold. The fair value answers a different question, and on it the shares are overvalued: on the Low uncertainty band the line sits at US$239.75, and the price is well past it. The valuation zone is the one place a fair value is used on this page, and it is labelled as such. A valuation is a set of assumptions, and letting one move a sector-relative rating would make that rating mean something different for every reader.
risk: We assign Apple a Low uncertainty rating, built from six of six measurable drivers. None of them reads wide. Two read moderate, the spread across the valuation models and the volatility of the share price, and the other four are contained, which places the rating at the bottom of the scale. The model spread is narrow partly by construction: the three models set aside as not describing the company, the lowest of them at US$26.93, are outside it, and the ten that remain agree more closely.

Taking them in turn: the valuation models span 24.9% between the upper and lower quartile, against the estimate, and share price volatility of 27.2%, annualised from weekly returns over the past year, both read moderate. Beta of 1.09 is contained — the shares move with the market rather than ahead of it. Net debt of 0.3x EBITDA is contained by any standard. Net margin variability of 9.9% against its own average is contained, and consensus dispersion of 0.5% between the high and low estimate for the current year is very tight indeed.

That last figure is worth pausing on. Thirty analysts arriving within half a percent of each other on this year's earnings is not a sign that the future is knowable; it is a sign that this company guides carefully and that the sell side has learned to follow the guidance. The 100% beat rate across thirteen scored quarters is the same fact seen from another angle. Neither tells you anything about the years the guidance does not cover.

The company-specific concentrations are the risks the drivers above do not capture. iPhone is 50.4% of revenue and Greater China is 15.5%, and those exposures are not independent of each other. The shares have fallen 13.8% peak to trough inside the last year, and have returned 31.9% over twelve months while lagging the sector by 4.8% — a reminder that the recent move has been the market's more than the company's.

The honest limit on this rating is what the method cannot see. Morningstar sets its equivalent from an analyst's scenario analysis of the business. This one is measured from market and accounting data, which catches a volatile, geared or hard-to-forecast company reliably and will miss anything that has not yet appeared in the numbers: a regulatory decision on the App Store economics, an adverse ruling on the default-search arrangements, a supply chain interruption, a product transition that does not take. None of those would move a single driver above until after the fact.
capital: We assign Apple a Standard capital allocation rating, scoring 4.0 of 6 across the three legs. The balance sheet reads adequate, investment exceptional, and shareholder distributions adequate. The middle leg is the one carrying the rating, and the two adequates are both consequences of the same deliberate policy rather than of any weakness in the business.

On the balance sheet, the company holds US$62.38b of cash against US$84.28b of total debt, leaving net debt at 0.3x EBITDA. The Altman Z-score is 12.49 and the Piotroski score 9 of 9, both about as strong as those screens go. What pulls the leg to adequate rather than sound is the current ratio of 1.00, which ranks in the bottom 9% of the sector, and equity funding just 28% of assets. This is a balance sheet run for efficiency, not for comfort.

The investment leg is where the rating is earned. Returns on capital sit 43% above their cost in the latest year and have averaged 23.9% above across the ten-year run. Research and development spending rose from US$10.05b to US$34.55b over that period while the operating margin widened from 27.8% to 32% — reinvestment at scale that has not diluted the returns it was funded from. There is no evidence here of capital being deployed into anything that earns less than it costs.

Distributions are large and consistent. The company returned US$106.1b to shareholders in the most recent filed year through dividends and buybacks combined, and the diluted share count has fallen 31.8% across the run. The dividend itself is a rounding error by comparison — a 0.3% yield on a 12.1% payout ratio — which makes the buyback effectively the entire distribution policy.

That US$106.1b represented 107.5% of free cash flow, and returning more than the business generated in the year is why the leg reads adequate rather than appropriate. It is not imprudent at this level of net debt and it is plainly accretive while returns on capital run at 51.9%: retiring stock funded at the margin by cheap debt, in a company earning five times its cost of capital, is arithmetic that works. It is worth naming as policy rather than as a one-off, because it is also the reason the current ratio and the equity base look as thin as they do.

One thing this rating does not assess is management. Timothy D. Cook leads the company, and tenure, succession, the judgement behind an acquisition and the quality of the board are not in the filings this report reads. Morningstar's equivalent rating rests heavily on exactly those. Ours rests on three measured legs and claims nothing beyond them.

note.headline: NVIDIA Takes Its Data Center Franchise Into the PC While the Price Runs Ahead of the Cash Flows
why: Data Center was US$193.7b of NVIDIA’s US$215.9b revenue in fiscal 2026, 89.7% of the company, up from US$10.6b four years earlier. That single line supplied 97% of all the revenue the company added over the period, and it is the reason operating profit rose from US$10.0b to US$130.4b.

On 7 October the business stepped outside the data center in a way it never has: RTX Spark, its first chip to run Windows as the main processor, went on sale in Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra and in machines from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo and MSI. It is a direct challenge to Intel’s place in premium laptops and to Apple’s MacBook Pro, which Microsoft names in its own marketing.

Our quant rating is Buy, grade B+, 3.46 of 5 across 76 ranked ratios. Financial health (A-, 4.42) and growth (A-, 4.05) carry it; valuation (C-, 1.66) is the only factor below the sector median, and even there the trailing P/E of 28.8x sits at the sector median of 28.6x and well under the peer median of 90.3x.
Our fair value estimate is US$190.64, the median of the ten models that fit the company. At US$229.28 the shares trade at 1.20 times it, inside the fairly valued band on a Medium uncertainty rating.
note.bottomLine: We rate NVIDIA Buy on the quant scale, grade B+, 3.46 of 5, and read the business as wide-moat, with returns on capital above their cost in 9 of the last 10 filed years and 48.7 points above it in the latest. The shares screen fairly valued at US$229.28 against a US$190.64 fair value estimate; they would read undervalued below US$133.45 and overvalued above US$257.37. What separates the price from our estimate is not the forecast, which we take as the consensus publishes it, but the discount rate: a beta of 2.22 makes the market charge NVIDIA 14.1% for its capital, and at that rate even the most optimistic published revenue path does not reach today’s price.

strategy: NVIDIA turned over US$303.0b in the trailing twelve months with 42k employees and converted 55.6% of revenue into net income in its last filed year. It is no longer a graphics company that also sells to data centers; it is a data center company that also sells graphics. Data Center is 89.7% of revenue, Gaming 7.4%, and the three remaining lines (professional visualization, automotive, and OEM and other) share what is left.

What it sells into the data center is a system rather than a chip: the GPU, the CPU beside it, the networking that ties thousands of them together, and the CUDA software layer that developers have written against for almost two decades. The shipments recorded this autumn show the shape of it. Supermicro began shipping Vera Rubin NVL72 racks on 23 September, CoreWeave put the same system into production for its first customer on 30 September, and AM Intelligence announced binding orders for 20,000 Rubin GPUs on 5 October. Each is a third party committing capital to the next NVIDIA generation before the current one has finished ramping.

The strategy for the next leg is to take that stack wherever AI runs. Two moves this year mark the edges. In September NVIDIA agreed to buy Hugging Face, the platform where open models are published, for US$12.93b, a quarter of one percent of its market value; in October it put RTX Spark, the GB10 superchip it has sold in DGX Spark mini-PCs for a year, into Windows laptops. One reaches up to the software developers choose models on, the other out to the machine on their desk.

Geographically the revenue is billed mostly in the United States, 69.3% in fiscal 2026, with China at US$19.68b. Billing location says where invoices go, not where chips end up, and export rules on advanced chips to China remain a live constraint: a contractor linked to Super Micro pleaded guilty on 9 October to diverting servers with NVIDIA chips there, a case that concerns its customers’ compliance rather than NVIDIA’s own.

Looking forward we take the consensus as published. Thirty-four analysts expect revenue to go from US$213.7b in fiscal 2026 to US$924.4b in fiscal 2029, roughly a fourfold increase in three years, at margins close to today’s. That path is the single largest assumption in everything below, and the consensus itself thins and widens in the outer years.
bulls: Data Center revenue went from US$10.6b to US$193.7b in four fiscal years and supplied 97% of all the revenue NVIDIA added, while gross margin rose from 64.9% to 71.1%: demand outran supply at prices customers kept paying.

Return on invested capital has exceeded its cost in 9 of the last 10 filed years, by 48.7 points in the latest; the company earns that while carrying net debt of 0.1x EBITDA and a current ratio of 4.59.

The platform is widening rather than narrowing: Rubin systems were shipping through third parties in September, Hugging Face brings the open-model layer in-house, and RTX Spark puts the full CUDA stack into Windows PCs for the first time.
bears: Concentration is extreme: 89.7% of revenue sits in one line sold to a small number of very large buyers, and those buyers are also designing their own accelerators.

The forecast needs revenue to roughly quadruple in three years; operating margin fell to 15.7% as recently as fiscal 2023, and the same operating leverage that built the profit will work in reverse if spending pauses.

At a 14.1% cost of capital, set by a beta of 2.22, every discounted cash flow model we build values the shares below the US$229.28 price except the two that exit on a sector EBITDA multiple; the market is paying for growth beyond the published consensus.
moat: We assign NVIDIA a wide economic moat. Return on invested capital has exceeded our estimate of the cost of that capital in 9 of the last 10 filed years, by an average of 20.2 points, and by 48.7 points in fiscal 2026. The one year it fell short was fiscal 2023, when gaming demand and crypto mining collapsed together and operating margin dropped to 15.7%. The recovery from that year is part of the evidence: a business without a moat does not come back from a downturn with a wider margin than it went in with.

The first source of the moat is the data center itself. Data Center revenue is US$193.7b, 89.7% of the company, and NVIDIA sells it as a whole system rather than a part: GPUs, the Grace CPU, NVLink and the Mellanox networking that connects tens of thousands of chips into one machine. A buyer comparing a rival accelerator is comparing a chip against a rack, and the rack is what the customer actually has to make work.

The second and deeper source is CUDA. Almost every AI framework, library and model in production was written and tuned against NVIDIA’s software layer, and the developers who know it are the scarce resource in the industry. That is a switching cost that sits with the customer’s engineers rather than in a contract, which is why it survives price increases. The gross margin is the measurement of it: 71.1% in fiscal 2026, against 64.9% four years earlier, on a product line that grew eighteenfold over the same period. A company selling a commodity cannot raise its margin while multiplying its volume.

The moat is now being extended into the PC, and this is where it reaches competitors that have never faced NVIDIA directly. RTX Spark brings a Blackwell GPU with up to 6,144 CUDA cores, a 20-core Grace CPU and up to 128 GB of unified memory into a Windows laptop, with Microsoft as design partner and five PC makers shipping on day one. For Intel, whose processors are in most Windows laptops, it is the first serious alternative at the premium end, backed by the one company whose software developers already use. For Apple it attacks the claim the MacBook Pro has owned since the move to its own silicon, that unified memory makes a Mac the best machine to run AI locally; Microsoft is paying MacBook Pro owners up to US$1,000 to switch and publishing its own benchmarks of two to six times the local AI speed. Those benchmarks are the vendors’ and untested, and no revenue figure for RTX Spark has been disclosed, so this is a widening of the moat to watch rather than one to count yet.

What could narrow it is visible in the same customers. The largest buyers of data center GPUs, the cloud platforms and model builders, are also designing their own accelerators with Broadcom and others, and Broadcom’s chief executive has said custom silicon is on pace to match GPU units in volume next year. Custom chips win on cost for a known, stable workload; they lose where the model changes every few months and the software has to follow. NVIDIA’s defence is to stay where the change is fastest, which is also why it bought Hugging Face and why it keeps the platform open to every accelerator.

The limit on this rating is the usual one: it is a measurement of ten years that have already happened, nine of them above the line. A wide moat elsewhere is a forecast that excess returns last twenty years. Nothing in the filed accounts can prove that, and the most concentrated revenue base of any company of this size is the reason to hold the forecast more loosely than the record.
fairValue: Our fair value estimate is US$190.64 a share, the median of ten models. Thirteen were run; three, the price/book, price/sales and EV/revenue multiples, were set aside because a sector multiple assumes sector economics and NVIDIA’s are not close: it earns a 110% return on equity against a thin book, and keeps 64% of sales as profit against a sector median of 9%. Those three valued the shares between US$34.84 and US$54.86, which says nothing about NVIDIA and a great deal about the method.

The profit drivers are not hard to find. Between fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2026 operating profit rose by US$120.3b. US$70.5b of that came from selling more at the old margin, almost all of it in Data Center, and US$49.8b from the margin itself widening from 37.3% to 60.4%. The margin came from two places at once: gross margin up from 64.9% to 71.1% on pricing and a richer mix, and research and development falling from 19.6% of revenue to 8.6% even as the spending rose. That second effect is operating leverage, and it is the reason the company keeps compounding profit faster than revenue.

Gaming was not dropped to make room for AI. It grew from US$12.5b to US$16.0b over the same four years; it was simply outgrown, falling from 46% of revenue to 7%. The PC now returns as a strategic market through RTX Spark rather than through gaming cards, and if it succeeds it will appear in a line that is small today. The fiscal 2023 trough, when operating margin fell to 15.7%, is the reminder of what happens to this cost structure when one large market stalls.

Which models deserve weight. The two 10-year discounted cash flows, at US$175.23 and US$176.67, are the most informative: they discount six years of analyst forecasts and four more faded to a 2.5% terminal rate, and only 46% of their value rests on the terminal year. The earnings multiples, EV/EBIT at US$204.62 and P/E at US$228.04, use sector medians of 21.6x and 28.6x and are conservative for a company growing this fast. The five-year EBITDA-exit model at US$296.03 is the least reliable, since 86% of its value is a terminal multiple applied to fiscal 2030 EBITDA.

The parameter that matters most is the discount rate. Every cash flow model uses 14.1%, built from a cost of equity of 14.2% that reflects a beta of 2.22: the market prices NVIDIA’s risk at more than twice the index’s, and charges for it. At that rate the bull case, which reruns the cash flows on the highest revenue any analyst publishes, reaches US$199.34, still below the price. The price therefore implies one of three things: growth that lasts beyond the consensus horizon, margins wider than the consensus, or a lower cost of capital than the share price’s own volatility suggests.

None of this feeds the quant rating, which grades NVIDIA against its sector and is Buy. The fair value answers a different question, and on it the shares are fairly valued, 20.3% above our estimate and inside the Medium-uncertainty band.
risk: We assign NVIDIA a Medium uncertainty rating from six of six measurable drivers. Beta, at 2.22, is the one that reads wide; share price volatility of 36%, the 35.1% spread across the valuation models and the 38.8% variability of the net margin read moderate; net debt and the dispersion of analysts’ earnings estimates are contained.

The concentration is the risk the drivers do not capture. Data Center is 89.7% of revenue, sold to a short list of very large buyers whose capital budgets move together, and whose own chip programs are the most direct competitive threat. A pause in that spending would meet a cost structure built for growth: the fiscal 2023 margin of 15.7% is what that looked like the last time.

Supply is a second constraint rather than a risk to demand. The company’s chips are made at TSMC on the most advanced nodes, the same capacity Apple called its binding constraint on its July earnings call, and they depend on high-bandwidth memory from a small group of suppliers whose prices have risen sharply this year.

Policy is the third. Export controls on advanced chips to China have already cut what NVIDIA can sell there, and enforcement now reaches its customers: a contractor linked to Super Micro pleaded guilty on 9 October to diverting servers with NVIDIA chips to China. Revenue billed to China was US$19.68b in fiscal 2026.

This rating is measured from market and accounting data, which catches a volatile, hard-to-forecast business reliably and will miss a contingent risk that has not reached the numbers: a regulatory ruling, an antitrust review of the Hugging Face purchase, or a large customer moving a workload to its own silicon.
capital: We assign NVIDIA an Exemplary capital allocation rating. The balance sheet is sound, with net debt of 0.1x EBITDA, a current ratio of 4.59 and an Altman Z-score of 41.35; investment is exceptional, with returns on capital 48.7 points above their cost; and distributions are appropriate.

The company returned US$41.06b to shareholders last year, 42.5% of free cash flow, almost all of it through buybacks; the dividend takes 3.5% of earnings. In the filed year buybacks were US$40.09b against US$974.0m of dividends.

Investment has stayed light for the size of the business. Capital spending was 2.8% of revenue in fiscal 2026, because NVIDIA designs and TSMC manufactures; the money goes into research and development, acquisitions such as Hugging Face, and stakes in customers and partners across the AI build-out. Those stakes are worth watching: they make some customers also investees, and the line between demand and financing is one investors are now asking about.

Jensen Huang has led the company since he co-founded it in 1993. This rating makes no assessment of management beyond the three measured legs, but founder-led continuity through four product cycles is part of how the record above was built.
